html:
The Kingdom of Kongo was a kingdom in west Central Africa, south of the lower Congo River, in what is now northern Angola and the western Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its king, the manikongo, ruled from Mbanza Kongo from the late 1300s.

The king appointed nobles to govern its provinces and collected tribute in cloth, ivory and nzimbu shells, which served as money.

Portuguese ships under Diogo Cão reached the Congo River in 1483. In 1491 King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised as João I. His son Afonso I (ruled 1509 to 1542) made Catholicism the state religion, sent nobles to study in Lisbon and saw his son Henrique made a bishop. Kongo kings wrote to the kings of Portugal and to the popes as fellow Christian rulers. Afonso also complained in his letters about Portuguese traders seizing his subjects, as Kongo was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade.

Relations soured after the Portuguese founded Luanda to the south in 1576. At the Battle of Mbwila in 1665 a Portuguese army killed King António I, and Kongo fell into decades of civil war. A young prophet, Beatriz Kimpa Vita, preached reunion and was burned in 1706. Pedro IV reunited the kingdom, but it never regained its old power. In the 1800s it became a Portuguese vassal, and Portugal abolished the title after a revolt in 1914.
